today in my perambulations in historic athens i came upon a happy gathering enjoying the fruits of civilization. a mini-beehive of industry on an otherwise hushed sunday morning. the knackers car-boot has nothing on this free for all of recycling nirvana, every imaginable item is on sale, laid out on a checkerboard of assorted tarps and blankets, in the rain, no cover. the charming denizens of this athenian outpost wend their days diligently sorting through the detritus (or detritus, however you like) of the modern civilized metropolis. happily pursuing the sale of a "twenty lepta" second hand bag, pair of shoes or a showey trinket. jackets and trainers bring one whole euro. there is grilled mystery meat and fried doughy substance with sugar for a quid or two. the ecclectic crowd has a frenetic feel about it, as if in a hurry to some important meeting or rushing home to make the school run...people push and shoulder their way through the crowd dragging improbably shaped bags stuffed to bursting. like some post-apocalyptic hollywood set the crowd mingles and surges as trucks and trikes jockey for position amongst stalls with only just barely agreed upon boundries in a constant battle for pride of place and notice. diesel fumes mingle with smell of burning fat and over-used cooking oil. two north african women huff by, lugging a large bundle of clothing and bits, they struggle through the crowd chastising one another in some out of place native tongue. "keep it out of the mud!"...."i'm trying, it's heavy.." i chat with two quick fingered shutter-bugs from the local art school; "what's going on around here?" i ask "oh, it's a big flea market," her english quick as a muffin, "but you have to get here really early if you want to find anything good." "of course..." they don't seem worried about their expensive cameras and designer bags... like pickers everywhere these people form natural affinities, and a class system of sorts. the car parts and tyre guys are up against the wall with their nebulous assortment of suspicious 'rescued' parts, the raincoat and umbrella lady snatched a great location and is doing a brisk business in last years fashion and plastic coverings from asia. as i wandered into the homewares and china area it became clear there was a steady stream of people with bundles and suitcases coming from up the street, all carrying the same thing, clothing. as i traced this line of busy ragpickers i became more and more curious as to the source of this wealth of second hand clothing being sold for such astonishingly cheap prices. two blocks down and two blocks over i had my answer, two double sized construction skips overflowing with nothing but donated clothes, heaps and bundles piled in the rain with people delving through it, grabbing at anything that might sell for five or ten cents. like some modern day gold miner a pair of shoes with the laces tied together seem to be buried pirate treasure to the skinny teen assiduously perched on the summit of this vesuvius of vestments, he tosses the booty down to his mate and turns back to his task. the search goes on. back here, away from the buyers and the hectic feel of the market the mood is more relaxed, children play in the street using some building material as props to fulfill their fantasy world. sure enough in the next block is another large skip, this time full of construction debris. the work here is more serious and the workers older, but using the term 'men' would be an untruth. there is broken glass and dangerous materials everywhere, jagged worms of rebar snake their way out of chunks of broken concrete. here a sorting, of a kind, is done, aluminium and steel taking pride of place with other base metals are turned over to the lads with four wheel pickups, this job to heavy for the little trykes that balance wild loads of scrap metal, glass and plastic. they seem content, these real world survivalists, content to gather the unwanted, unused, outgrown and out of fashion leavings from a very different world. a world that lies not just on the other side of the tracks in athens or london or paris but unreachable and totally unimaginable to millions of people in countries that are the victims of an imperialist set of proxy wars that date back well over two hundred years and a financial system no better than a crooked casino with stacked decks. it seems normal to these people, this constant struggle to survive, their sunday perhaps enhanced by a warm meal for a change, their week made slightly more bearable by five or ten euros, perhaps a new pair of trousers for a growing child or a new stuffed bear for the youngest. and what about us? does it keep us warm at night knowing we gave our second best jumper to the church charity? do we sleep better in our cosy flats knowing that last years trainers went to 'the less fortunate'? why do we continue to empower the people and institutions that thrive on war and conflict, the multi-national mega-corps that consistently put profit before people? simple; "it looks good from my house."

today in my perambulations in historic athens i came upon a happy gathering enjoying the fruits of civilization. a mini-beehive of industry on an otherwise hushed sunday morning. the knackers car-boot has nothing on this free for all of recycling nirvana, every imaginable item is on sale, laid out on a checkerboard of assorted tarps and blankets, in the rain, no cover. the charming denizens of this athenian outpost wend their days diligently sorting through the detritus (or detritus, however you like) of the modern civilized metropolis. happily pursuing the sale of a "twenty lepta" second hand bag, pair of shoes or a showey trinket. jackets and trainers bring one whole euro. there is grilled mystery meat and fried doughy substance with sugar for a quid or two. the ecclectic crowd has a frenetic feel about it, as if in a hurry to some important meeting or rushing home to make the school run...people push and shoulder their way through the crowd dragging improbably shaped bags stuffed to bursting. like some post-apocalyptic hollywood set the crowd mingles and surges as trucks and trikes jockey for position amongst stalls with only just barely agreed upon boundries in a constant battle for pride of place and notice. diesel fumes mingle with smell of burning fat and over-used cooking oil. two north african women huff by, lugging a large bundle of clothing and bits, they struggle through the crowd chastising one another in some out of place native tongue. "keep it out of the mud!"...."i'm trying, it's heavy.." i chat with two quick fingered shutter-bugs from the local art school; "what's going on around here?" i ask "oh, it's a big flea market," her english quick as a muffin, "but you have to get here really early if you want to find anything good." "of course..." they don't seem worried about their expensive cameras and designer bags... like pickers everywhere these people form natural affinities, and a class system of sorts. the car parts and tyre guys are up against the wall with their nebulous assortment of suspicious 'rescued' parts, the raincoat and umbrella lady snatched a great location and is doing a brisk business in last years fashion and plastic coverings from asia. as i wandered into the homewares and china area it became clear there was a steady stream of people with bundles and suitcases coming from up the street, all carrying the same thing, clothing. as i traced this line of busy ragpickers i became more and more curious as to the source of this wealth of second hand clothing being sold for such astonishingly cheap prices. two blocks down and two blocks over i had my answer, two double sized construction skips overflowing with nothing but donated clothes, heaps and bundles piled in the rain with people delving through it, grabbing at anything that might sell for five or ten cents. like some modern day gold miner a pair of shoes with the laces tied together seem to be buried pirate treasure to the skinny teen assiduously perched on the summit of this vesuvius of vestments, he tosses the booty down to his mate and turns back to his task. the search goes on. back here, away from the buyers and the hectic feel of the market the mood is more relaxed, children play in the street using some building material as props to fulfill their fantasy world. sure enough in the next block is another large skip, this time full of construction debris. the work here is more serious and the workers older, but using the term 'men' would be an untruth. there is broken glass and dangerous materials everywhere, jagged worms of rebar snake their way out of chunks of broken concrete. here a sorting, of a kind, is done, aluminium and steel taking pride of place with other base metals are turned over to the lads with four wheel pickups, this job to heavy for the little trykes that balance wild loads of scrap metal, glass and plastic. they seem content, these real world survivalists, content to gather the unwanted, unused, outgrown and out of fashion leavings from a very different world. a world that lies not just on the other side of the tracks in athens or london or paris but unreachable and totally unimaginable to millions of people in countries that are the victims of an imperialist set of proxy wars that date back well over two hundred years and a financial system no better than a crooked casino with stacked decks. it seems normal to these people, this constant struggle to survive, their sunday perhaps enhanced by a warm meal for a change, their week made slightly more bearable by five or ten euros, perhaps a new pair of trousers for a growing child or a new stuffed bear for the youngest. and what about us? does it keep us warm at night knowing we gave our second best jumper to the church charity? do we sleep better in our cosy flats knowing that last years trainers went to 'the less fortunate'? why do we continue to empower the people and institutions that thrive on war and conflict, the multi-national mega-corps that consistently put profit before people? simple; "it looks good from my house."
